headline: Microsoft exec called AI scraping 'the largest theft of labor in human history'
summary: Internal documents from the NYT lawsuit reveal Microsoft and OpenAI knew their AI training practices posed an "existential threat" to publishers, with one exec calling it "the largest theft of labor in human history."
details: A top Microsoft executive privately described AI training practices by companies as "the largest theft of labor in human history," according to newly unsealed documents from The New York Times' lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft. OpenAI's own leadership also acknowledged their AI models posed an "existential threat" to publishers.

Internal Microsoft data showed its Copilot "answer engine" caused click-through rates for The New York Times' domain to drop by as much as 93% compared to traditional Bing search. An internal presentation described this decline as a "doom loop" that would "hurt the performance of our models and the entire web."

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella testified that paywalled content should be licensed for AI training, stating he would have required OpenAI to retrain models if he knew they scraped paywalled information. OpenAI President Greg Brockman described the models as "excellent at news," and Nadella agreed they substitute direct website visits.

The lawsuit filing details the scale of copying, revealing OpenAI's mid-training datasets contained over 91,692 copies of works from NYT, Daily News, and Center for Investigative Reporting. A Common Crawl-derived dataset included more than 2 million documents from nytimes.com alone.

OpenAI employees allegedly devised a plan to circumvent paywalls without detection. An OpenAI researcher informed Brockman about a "hack to get around nytimes paywall," to which Brockman replied, "ah nice."

Counsel for the New York Daily News stated that the evidence "shows that OpenAI and Microsoft knew that what they were doing was wrong." This information challenges OpenAI's fair use defense, particularly regarding harm to the market for original work.

headline_marked: [[Napster wants to digitally clone teachers]] in new education AI pivot
headline: Napster wants to digitally clone teachers in new education AI pivot
summary: The iconic Napster brand has pivoted to AI, partnering with Gems Education in Dubai to develop digital personas and AI agents, including "digital twins" of teachers for 24/7 student support.
details: Napster, the name synonymous with early digital music, has returned as an artificial intelligence platform. It has partnered with Gems Education in Dubai to build AI agents and digital personas for classrooms, including "digital twins" of teachers.

The original Napster launched in 1999 as a peer-to-peer music-sharing service. After various iterations, it was acquired by Infinite Reality in 2025 for $207 million and pivoted to AI, shutting down its music streaming service in January.

Napster is establishing a regional hub in Dubai, led by Samuel Huber, formerly of Landvault. Huber states the new Napster's ethos is about giving power to users over data and intelligence, challenging the power of large AI model companies.

Proof-of-concept projects with Gems will include digitalizing instructors, gamified learning, AI-assisted content creation, and classroom simulations. The first phase will be at the Gems School of Research and Innovation.

Napster Learn, its AI-powered system, will provide resources. Digital twins of teachers, trained on their materials, will offer around-the-clock online support, allowing students to ask questions and refine concepts at their own pace.

Teachers will receive insights into student questions, helping identify areas for additional support. Huber emphasizes that AI agents augment teachers rather than replacing them, creating a more natural interaction experience.

Napster states student data will remain within the country and can be hosted on private servers. The company also confirms it does not use user data to train its AI models, addressing privacy concerns.

Despite fears of job displacement, Huber argues that educators must learn to use AI smartly for augmentation. He believes AI can become a tool to enhance human capabilities, similar to word processors.
